title: Birth–Death Processes and M/M/1 Queues
breadcrumb: Stochastic processes → Birth–death processes → M/M/1 queues
engineName: Track one-step births and deaths, find equilibrium probabilities, then translate the birth–death model into queueing measures.
objectives: Represent a birth–death process using state-dependent birth and death rates.
Write the forward balance equations and identify stationary probabilities.
Derive the stationary distribution of an M/M/1 queue and its stability condition.
Calculate utilisation, idle probability, mean queue length, mean system size and waiting times.
Distinguish customers in the queue from customers in the whole system and apply Little’s law.

prereq.name: Poisson process and exponential waiting times
prereq.why: M/M/1 assumes Poisson arrivals and exponential service times.

prereq.name: Geometric series
prereq.why: The stationary M/M/1 probabilities form a geometric distribution.

prereq.name: Expectation and Little’s law
prereq.why: Queueing measures are long-run means linked by flow rate and time.

traps: Birth and death rates depend on the current state; do not assume constant rates unless specified.
For M/M/1, λ is the arrival rate and μ is the service rate.
A stationary distribution exists only when λ<μ; ρ=λ/μ must be below one.
P(N=n)=(1−ρ)ρⁿ includes n=0; the queue is empty with probability 1−ρ.
L is the mean number in the whole system; Lq excludes the customer in service.
W is time in the whole system; Wq is waiting time before service.
Use the same time unit for λ and μ.
howto: Define the state n, identify upward and downward transition rates, write local balance, normalise the stationary probabilities, check stability, and only then calculate queueing measures.

provenance: Original teaching material aligned to the Birth and death processes and M/M/1 queues items in UGC NET Statistics Unit IX. Practice questions are original and are not represented as official UGC NET PYQs.

sheet: A birth–death process moves n→n+1 at rate λ_n and n→n−1 at rate μ_n.
For n≥1, the forward equation is p'_n(t)=λ_{n−1}p_{n−1}(t)+(μ_{n+1})p_{n+1}(t)−(λ_n+μ_n)p_n(t).
Stationary local balance: π_n λ_n=π_{n+1} μ_{n+1}.
π_n=π_0∏_{k=0}^{n−1}(λ_k/μ_{k+1}); choose π_0 so probabilities sum to one.
M/M/1: arrivals Poisson(λ), service times Exp(μ), one server, FCFS, infinite capacity and population.
ρ=λ/μ; a stationary distribution requires ρ<1.
tricks: If ρ≥1, do not calculate stationary M/M/1 means as if equilibrium existed.
The probability of n customers is geometric over n=0,1,…, not a Poisson count.
Check L−Lq=ρ: on average, this is the probability that the server is busy.
Check Little’s law independently: L/λ should equal W.
shortcuts: Given λ and μ, calculate ρ first; it decides stability and supplies every M/M/1 formula.
As ρ approaches one from below, queue length and waiting time grow rapidly.
remember: The first M in M/M/1 refers to Markovian (Poisson) arrivals; the second to exponential service; 1 is one server.
L and W include service; Lq and Wq exclude service.

scenes.title: Refresh rates, states and exponential times
scenes.objective: Recover the tools needed to read a birth–death model.
body: A continuous-time Markov chain changes state at random event times. In a birth–death process the state is a nonnegative integer: a birth increases it by one and a death decreases it by one.
A rate is an average event intensity per unit time. If a service rate is μ=5 per hour, the mean service time is 1/5 hour. An exponential waiting time with rate μ has survival probability e^(−μt).
The state is not necessarily a population of people: it may be customers in a system, machines operating, or another count. The meaning of a birth and death must be defined from the context.

items.ask: If the service rate is 4 customers per hour, what is the mean service time?
refresh: The reciprocal has units of hours.

items.ask: In a customer-count model, what does a transition n→n+1 represent?
refresh: The state records the number of customers.
An arrival increases that count by one.
A departure decreases it by one.

ask.q: Why must arrival and service rates use the same time unit?
ask.nudge: You will divide one rate by the other to obtain utilisation.

scenes.title: A changing population: births and deaths
body: Imagine a small population. When the process is in state n, births occur at rate λ_n and deaths occur at rate μ_n. The rates may depend on n.

A birth–death process can describe queue length: arrivals are births, service completions are deaths. In an M/M/1 queue, arrivals occur at constant rate λ and service completions occur at rate μ whenever at least one customer is present.
At state zero there is no customer to depart, so μ_0=0. This boundary condition prevents the process from moving to a negative state.

scenario.title: The queue changes one customer at a time
body: A repair desk has one technician. Customers arrive one at a time. When the desk is empty, an arrival changes the state from 0 to 1. When there are three customers in the system, a service completion changes the state from 3 to 2.
The arrival rate is λ=2 per hour. The technician completes service at rate μ=3 per hour whenever at least one customer is present.
This is a birth–death process with λ_n=2 for every n≥0 and μ_n=3 for n≥1, while μ_0=0.
scenario.q: What are the possible transitions from state 2?
scenario.answer: A birth 2→3 at rate 2 per hour and a death 2→1 at rate 3 per hour.

ask.q: Why is there no death transition from state zero?
ask.nudge: A departure requires a customer to be present.

blocks.body: In state n, births occur at rate λ_n and deaths at rate μ_n; set μ_0=0.

ask.q: What must be done after obtaining the stationary probabilities up to a constant?
ask.nudge: Use the fact that all state probabilities sum to one.

scenes.title: The M/M/1 queue: assumptions and stability
scenes.objective: Identify the M/M/1 model and its stability condition.

blocks.body: Poisson arrivals at rate λ; independent exponential service times at rate μ; one server; usually FCFS; infinite waiting room and population.
ρ=λ/μ. The server is busy a fraction ρ of long-run time.
A stationary distribution exists only if λ<μ, equivalently ρ<1.

This excludes the customer in service.
The difference equals the probability that the server is busy.

scenes.title: Waiting times and Little’s law
scenes.objective: Calculate W and Wq and link them to mean queue sizes.

blocks.body: L=λW and L_q=λW_q, for a stable system.

ask.nudge: The time in the whole system includes waiting plus service.

scenes.title: Guided problem: queue performance
scenes.objective: Solve an M/M/1 numerical question with diminishing hints.
scenes.problem: An M/M/1 queue receives 4 customers per hour and serves 6 per hour. Find the mean number in the system, mean queue length and mean time in the system.
hints: First calculate ρ=λ/μ and check it is below one.
Use W=1/(μ−λ); keep the time unit in hours.
scenes.answer: ρ=2/3; L=2; Lq=4/3; W=1/2 hour = 30 minutes.
solution: ρ=4/6=2/3, so the queue is stable.
W=1/(6−4)=1/2 hour. Little’s law gives λW=4×1/2=2.

scenario.title: Measure congestion
body: A clinic receives 4 patients per hour and one clerk registers patients at rate 6 per hour. Under the M/M/1 assumptions, ρ=2/3.
The average number in the system is L=2 patients, while the average number waiting is Lq=4/3. The average time from arrival until leaving is W=1/(6−4)=0.5 hour.
These are long-run averages. They do not mean every patient waits exactly 30 minutes.
scenario.q: What is the average time spent in the system?

ask.q: Why is the answer an average rather than a promise about each patient?
ask.nudge: Queue lengths and waiting times are random.

scenes.title: Trap check: stability, units and definitions
scenes.intro: Mark each claim true or false, then compare the reason.

items.claim: An M/M/1 queue is stable when λ<μ.
items.why: The utilisation ρ=λ/μ must be below one.
P₀=1−ρ; ρ is the busy probability.

items.claim: Lq includes the customer currently receiving service.
items.why: Lq counts only those waiting; L counts everyone in the system.
W is time in the whole system.

items.claim: If λ=μ, the stationary geometric distribution is valid.
items.why: At ρ=1 the geometric probabilities cannot be normalised.

ask.q: Which first calculation should you always make before applying queue formulas?
ask.nudge: It tells you whether a stationary queue exists.
